SOAP Clinical Note

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: Intensely itchy, red, sore skin rash × 4 days affecting chest, hands, and antecubital fossae; interferes with sleep and concentration at work.
- History of presenting illness:
  • Onset 4 days ago, progressive itching.  
  • Tried OTC topical steroid cream last night – no relief.  
  • Tried OTC antihistamines previously – no relief.  
  • No bleeding, pus, or systemic symptoms (no fever, cough, dyspnea, bowel/urinary changes).  
  • No known trigger identified; no recent change in soaps/clothing noted.
- Past medical history: Atopic dermatitis/eczema (previous episodes limited to arms); remote history of asthma (resolved).
- Medications: None regular. Recent OTC topical steroid cream (dose/route/frequency not documented). Recent OTC antihistamines (name/dose/frequency not documented).
- Social history: 31-year-old male; lives with flatmates; project manager at pharmaceutical company; non-smoker; drinks a few beers per week.
- Allergies: Denies drug or other allergies.

Objective:
- Limited virtual visual inspection only; provider reports rash appears consistent with previous eczema flare (exact description not documented).
- No vitals provided.
- No investigations performed.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Diffuse pruritic rash
   - Assessment: Likely eczema (atopic dermatitis) flare.
   - Differential: Contact dermatitis, psoriasis, fungal infection.
   - Investigations planned: None at present; patient to keep diary of potential triggers (soaps, fabrics, activities).
   - Treatment planned:
     • Prescribe higher-potency topical corticosteroid (specific agent/strength not documented) for affected areas for 7–10 days.  
     • Prescribe emollient for bath/shower use; liberal application multiple times daily.  
     • Prescribe Fexofenadine (dose/frequency not documented) for pruritus; advise trial of other antihistamines if needed.  
     • Counsel on gentle skin care, avoiding harsh soaps, hot water, and known irritants.
   - Follow-up: Return in 1 week if no improvement or sooner if worsening; consider dermatology referral if refractory.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: Detailed skin examination description, vitals, specific prescription details (drug name/strength/dose/frequency), complete medication reconciliation.  
● No internal transcript conflicts noted.  
● Transcript quality: Several audio dropouts; clinician–patient audio clarity poor, limiting detail capture.
